(Almost) Ruling Out SETH Lower Bounds for All-Pairs Max-Flow

Ohad Trabelsi<sup>∗</sup> <sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup>Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago. Email: `ohadt@ttic.edu`

November 12, 2024

**Abstract**

The All-Pairs Max-Flow problem has gained significant popularity in the last two decades, and many results are known regarding its fine-grained complexity. Despite this, wide gaps remain in our understanding of the time complexity for several basic variants of the problem, including for directed or undirected input graphs that are edge- or node-capacitated, and where the capacities are unit or arbitrary. In this paper, we aim to bridge these gaps by providing algorithms, conditional lower bounds, and non-reducibility results. Notably, we show that for most problem settings, deterministic reductions based on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) cannot rule out \(O(n^{4-\varepsilon})\) time algorithms for some small constant \(\varepsilon>0\), under a hypothesis called NSETH.

To obtain our results for undirected graphs with unit node-capacities (aka All-Pairs Vertex Connectivity), we design a new _randomized Las Vegas_ \(O\big(m^{2+o(1)}\big)\) time combinatorial algorithm. This is our main technical result, improving over the recent \(O\big(m^{11/5+o(1)}\big)\) time _Monte Carlo_ algorithm [Huang et al., S 2023] and matching their _m_<sup>2-_o_(1)</sup> lower bound (up to subpolynomial factors), thus essentially settling the time complexity for this setting of the problem.

## 1 Introduction

The maximum _st_-flow problem, denoted Max-Flow, has been extensively studied in theoretical computer science for almost 70 years. This problem has become a key tool in algorithm design, with numerous applications of the problem and its techniques \[AMO93, FF56, AHK12, WL93\]. In a recent breakthrough, \[CKL<sup>+</sup>22, vdBCP<sup>+</sup>23\] gave an almost linear \(\hat{O}(m)\) time algorithm for the problem <sup>1,2,3</sup>. But what if we desire to find the Max-Flow value for all pairs? This problem is named All-Pairs Max-Flow, and the naive approach for it always works: simply apply a Max-Flow routine for every pair of nodes, thus resulting in an \(n^2\cdot m^{1+o(1)}\) time algorithm. Then the following question arises:

**_Q1_**_: Can All-Pairs Max-Flow be solved faster than the naive approach?_

_Alternatively, can we show conditional lower bounds?_

In the main variants of All-Pairs Max-Flow considered in the literature, the input graphs may be:

• directed or undirected,<tbc>

• edge-capacitated or node-capacitated, and<tbc>

• with unit-capacities, also called _connectivities_, or with arbitrary (usually polynomially-bounded) capacities.

It turns out that undirected graphs with edge capacities are particularly easy to solve, as a recent exciting line of work \[LP20, LP21, AKT21b, AKT21a, LPS21\] on Gomory-Hu tree<sup>4</sup> construction culminated with an almost linear \(\hat{O}(m)\) time algorithm \[AKL<sup>+</sup>22, ALPS23\]. However, the remaining variants are unlikely to be solved in almost linear time since hardness results are known for them (see  1), and so henceforth we call them _the hard variants_. In this context, the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)<sup>5</sup> \[IPZ01\] has been particularly useful, proving _n_<sup>3-_o_(1)</sup> time conditional lower bounds for hard variants in sparse \(m=\tilde{O}(n)\) graphs with (node or edge) capacities \[KT18, AKT20a\], and an _n_<sup>3-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bound for dense _m=O(n_<sup>2</sup>) graphs with unit edge- capacities.

Despite the lower bounds mentioned, the answer to **_Q1_** is positive in some restricted cases. For unit capacities in hard variants where either the input graph is sparse or the desired flow value is bounded, nontrivial algorithms are known. These include a network-coding based \(\tilde{O}(m^\omega)\) time algorithm for directed graphs with unit edge-capacities \[CLL13\], an \((nk)^\omega\) time adaptation of the latter to the _k_-bounded version of unit node-capacities (i.e., where the flow value is bounded by _k_), and an \(\hat{O}(mk^3)\) time algorithm for the _k_-bounded version of undirected graphs with unit node-capacities. The latter was obtained through an adaptation of an approximate Gomory-Hu tree algorithm \[LP21\] and employing an isolating cut lemma \[LP20, AKT21b, LNP<sup>+</sup>21\]. Very recently, via a high-degree low-degree method previously used in the context of Gomory-Hu trees \[AKT20a\], the \(\hat{O}(mk^3)\) algorithm above was adapted to an \(\hat{O}(m^{11/5})\) time algorithm for the unbounded version \[HLSW23\]. Still, in spite of extensive research, the naive approach remains the fastest algorithm for general dense graphs in all hard variants, while no matching conditional lower bounds are known. A relaxed phrasing of **_Q1_** restricts attention to combinatorial algorithms.<sup>6</sup>

<sup>1</sup>Henceforth, _n_ denotes the number of nodes, and _m_ the number of edges in an input graph. <sup>2</sup>\(\hat{O}(\cdot)\) hides _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> factors and \(\tilde{O}(\cdot)\) hides polylog(_n_) factors. <sup>3</sup>We say that a time bound _T(m_) is almost linear if it is bounded by _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> <sup>4</sup>This is a data structure that succinctly represents all min _st_-cuts in an input undirected graph with edge capacities. <sup>5</sup>SETH postulates that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an integer _k\>_0 such that _k_-SAT requires \(\Omega(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n})\) time. <sup>6</sup>_combinatorial algorithms_ commonly refers to algorithms avoiding fast matrix multiplication as a subroutine.

**_Q2:_** _What is the time complexity of All-Pairs Max-Flow when restricted to combinatorial algorithms?_

A typical hope is that this restriction would facilitate better conditional lower bounds. Indeed, at least for dense graphs, **_Q2_** is settled. By a reduction from the problem of detecting a 4-clique in a graph, it was shown \[AGI<sup>+</sup>19\] that all directed variants are unlikely to admit \(O(n^{4-\varepsilon})\) time combinatorial algorithms. Later, this technique was extended to undirected graphs with unit node- capacities \[HLSW23\], implying an _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bound against combinatorial algorithms for them as well. This result finally established that _no_ hard variant can be solved faster than the naive approach by a combinatorial algorithm, at least when the input graph is dense. Notably, all these _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bounds can also be expressed as _m_<sup>2-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bounds for all _m_ (accomplished by simply adding isolated nodes). This still leaves a gap for less dense graphs in various settings, including undirected graphs with unit node-capacities, for which the current upper bound is \(min\{\hat{O}(n^2\cdot m),\hat{O}(m^{11/5})\}\) (see Figure 1).

## 1.1 A New Algorithm for Graphs with Unit Node-Capacities

In our main result we resolve **_Q2_** for this setting across all densities by closing the gap with the known conditional lower bound against combinatorial algorithms (see also Figure 1), settling the time complexity of All-Pairs Max-Flow in these settings.

**Theorem 1.1.** _There is a randomized Las Vegas algorithm that given an undirected graph G_=(_V,E_) _with unit node-capacities, makes_ \(\tilde{O}(m)\) _calls to Max-Flow in G and spends_ \(\tilde{O}(mn)\) _time outside of these calls, and can:_

• _construct a data structure of size_ \(\tilde{O}\left(m^{3/2}\right)\) _that stores a set_ C _of_ \(\tilde{O}(m)\) _vertex-cut separators_<sup>7</sup>_, such that given a queried pair_ \(u,v\in V\) _outputs in_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _time a pointer to an optimal uv- separator in_ C.<tbc>

• _construct a data structure of size_ \(\tilde{O}(m)\) _that given a queried pair_ \(u,v\in V\) _outputs in_ \(\tilde{O}(Max-Flow(u,v))\) _time_<sup>8</sup> _the value Max-Flow(u,v_) _(or simply in_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _time in an alternative Monte Carlo version)._

To obtain this bound, we depart from the recent practice of using element-connectivity<sup>9</sup> for constructing vertex-connectivity data structures \[PSY22, HLSW23\], and adapt an algorithm previously employed for \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate All-Pairs Max-Flow on undirected, edge-capacitated graphs \[AKT20a\]. Note that our algorithm is Las Vegas, unlike many of the recent algorithms for All-Pairs Max-Flow which are Monte Carlo \[PSY22, AKL<sup>+</sup>22, HLSW23, ALPS23\]. This algorithm is also combinatorial, and runs in \(\hat{O}(m^2)\) time using the recent near linear \(\hat{O}(m)\) time Max-Flow algorithm \[CKL<sup>+</sup>22, vdBCP<sup>+</sup>23\], improving on the recent \(\hat{O}(m^{11/5})\) \[HLSW23\] time algorithm for the problem.

Following our resolution of **_Q2_** for unit node-capacities, the main open question remains: can we answer **_Q1_** by proving _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bounds for general algorithms too? Perhaps surprisingly, we establish a strong barrier to the possibility of such a result. We address **_Q1_** by<tbc>

We do so by designing subquartic nondeterministic algorithms<sup>11</sup> suited for each setting, and then applying a non-reducibility framework by Carmosino et al. \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16\]. First, we present a general method by which we obtain our nondeterministic algorithms. **Informal Theorem 1.2.** _Suppose there is a randomized Las Vegas algorithm for All-Pairs Max-Flow that makes q Max-Flow calls on input graphs G_=(_V,E_) _and spends_ \(\hat{O}(t)\) _time outside of these calls, and let_ \(\mu\) _be a volume upper bound on the maximum st-flow in G, for all pairs_ \(s,t\in V\) _. Note that for \(\omega=2\), this time becomes \(\hat{O}(q\cdot\mu+qn+t)\). In the remaining of this section we present our non-reducibility results for each variant.

## 1.2.1 Unit Node-Capacities

For undirected graphs with unit node-capacities, we obtain the following non-reducibility bound by combining Theorem 1.2 with the natural _O(n_) flow volume bound and the algorithm in Theorem 1.1.

**Theorem 1.3.** _Under NSETH, for any fixed_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _there is no deterministic fine-grained reduction_ <sup>13</sup> _proving an_ \(\Omega(n^{\omega(log_nm,1,1)+\varepsilon})\) _SETH-based lower bound for All-Pairs Max-Flow on undirected graphs with unit node-capacities._

For \(\omega=2\), the bound becomes \(\Omega(mn^{1+\varepsilon})\). A question posed by \[HLSW23\] is whether conditional lower bounds for general algorithms could match their _m_<sup>2-_o_(1)</sup> lower bounds against combinatorial algorithms. Theorem 1.3 conditionally answers this question negatively, for SETH-based results. That said, we observe a SETH lower bound for this setting, which is obtained by a straightforward adaptation of the conditional lower bound in \[AKT20b\] for general node-capacities to the unit node-capacities case, together with a recently developed source-sink isolating gadget \[HLSW23\].

**Theorem 1.4.** _If for some fixed_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _All-Pairs Max-Flow on undirected graphs with unit node- capacities can be solved in time_ \(O(n^2+m^{3/2-\varepsilon})\) _then SETH is false._

## 1.2.2 General node-capacities.

For directed graphs with general node-capacities<sup>14</sup>, we obtain the following non-reducibility bound by combining Theorem 1.2 with the naive algorithm and our new flow volume bounds.

**Theorem 1.5.** _Under NSETH, for any fixed_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _there is no deterministic fine-grained reduction proving an_ \(\Omega(n^{\omega(2,1,1)+\varepsilon})\) _SETH-based lower bound for All-Pairs Max-Flow on directed graphs with node-capacities._

For \(\omega=2\), the bound becomes \(\Omega(n^{3+\varepsilon})\). This result indicates that even when the input graph is dense and directed, the existing _n_<sup>3-_o_(1)</sup> SETH lower bound \[AKT20b\], designed for sparse undirected graphs, is unlikely to be improved.

### 1.2.3 Directed edge-capacities.

Our last non-reducibility result is for directed graphs with unit edge-capacities. By combining Theorem 1.2 with the naive algorithm and a flow volume bound obtained by Karger and Levine \[KL98\] in the context of (single pair) Max-Flow algorithms, we show that no deterministic SETH-based reduction is likely to prove an _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bound for this setting.

**Theorem 1.6.** _Under NSETH, for any fixed_ \(\varepsilon,\varepsilon'>0\) _there is no deterministic fine-grained reduction proving an_ \(\Omega(n^{5/2+\varepsilon}\sqrt{m}+n^{\omega(2,1,1)+\varepsilon^\prime})\) _SETH-based lower bound for All-Pairs Max-Flow on directed graphs with unit edge-capacities._

For \(\omega=2\), the bound becomes \(\Omega(n^{5/2+\varepsilon}\sqrt{m})\). Combining our framework with Gusfield’s algorithm for Gomory-Hu trees \[Gus90\] immediately provides an _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time nondeterministic algorithm for All-Pairs Max-Flow in undirected graphs with unit edge-capacities. Although this algorithm may not be competitive given the \(\tilde{O}(m)\) time nondeterministic algorithm for Gomory-Hu tree construction \[AKT20a\], we still find this observation meaningful. Relatedly, a nondeterministic algorithm was the seed of inspiration for recent breakthroughs in randomized algorithms for this problem \[AKL<sup>+</sup>22, ALPS23\] (see \[AKT21b, AKT21a\] for discussions), and we believe that the same could happen to the nondeterministic algorithms presented in this paper.

Finally, for directed graphs with general edge-capacities, we could not prove a subquartic nondeterministic algorithm. However, as a consequence of Theorem 1.5, we conclude that a hypothetical deterministic fine-grained reduction from the edge-capacities setting to the node-capacities setting would imply the non-existence of an _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bound for the edge-capacities setting.

**Theorem 1.7.** _Suppose there exists a deterministic fine-grained reduction proving that an_ \(O(n^{4-\varepsilon})\) _time algorithm for All-Pairs Max-Flow on graphs with node-capacities implies an_ \(O(n^{4-\varepsilon^\prime})\) _algorithm for All-Pairs Max-Flow on directed graphs with edge-capacities, for some fixed_ \(\varepsilon,\varepsilon'>0\).

_Then, under NSETH, it is not possible to have an n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> _SETH-based lower bound for All-Pairs Max-Flow on directed graphs with edge-capacities._

Whether such a reduction exists is a well-known open problem in the field (see e.g. Open Problem 2 in \[AKT20b\]), and Theorem 1.7 points to a significant barrier to its positive resolution.

## 1.3 Technical Overview

Below we explain the ideas behind our randomized algorithm for undirected graphs with unit node- capacities. Then, we elaborate on our non-reducibility results.

### 1.3.1 An algorithm for undirected graph with unit node-capacities

#### High level ideas in the algorithm in \[AKT20a\]

One of the core ideas in the \((1+\varepsilon)\)- approximation algorithm for graphs with edge-capacities could be interpreted as the following: The minimum cuts between any three nodes can be captured by just two cuts. This is represented also by the following inequality for any set of nodes _u,v,w_,

\(\mathsf{Max-Flow}(u,v)\ge min\{\mathsf{Max-Flow}(u,w),\mathsf{Max-Flow}(v,w)\},\) (1.1)

which translates to the algorithmic insight that the minimum cuts between a randomly picked pivot and every other node can capture many more minimum cuts in the graph. More concretely, it was shown in \[AKT20a\] that the minimum cuts computed from a random (source) pivot _p_ to all other (sink) nodes \(u\in V\) can be used to partition _V_ as follows. Let \(S_{u,p}\subset V\) be the side of _u_ in<tbc>

<tbc>a minimum _pu_-cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_). Each node _u_ is then reassigned to a set \(S_{u^\prime,p}\) containing _u_, where nodes reassigned to the same \(S_{u^\prime,p}\) are grouped together. This partition satisfies that its biggest part is of expected size at most \(\frac{3}{4}n\), while preserving property (\*) below. This allows the algorithm to continue recursively with an _O_(log_n_) bound on the recursion-tree depth.

(\*) For every pair \(s'\in S_{i,p},t'\in S_{j,p}\) for \(i\neq j\), at least one of (_S<sub>i,p</sub>,S<sub>p,i</sub>_) or (_S<sub>j,p</sub>,S<sub>p,j</sub>_) corresponds in _G_ to a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate minimum \(s't'\)-cut.

Crucially, property (\*) ensures that the Max-Flow values between node pairs of different sets are determined at the current recursion step, i.e. one of the minimum cuts computed from _p_ captures the (approximated) value of Max-Flow(_u,v_), while handling the remaining pairs is postponed to a later stage.

## Barriers in adapting \[AKT20a\]

While symmetry holds in our case of undirected graphs with unit node-capacities, the same intuition is not directly applicable due to two main issues.

First, the triangle inequality 1.1 does not generally hold. This is illustrated by the example of nodes _p,u,v_ satisfying \(v\in C_{p,u}\) or \(u\in C_{p,v}\), where _C<sub>p,v</sub>_ is the separator in a minimum vertex _pv_-cut. This makes the presence of nodes in separators of many pairs an issue, as their own Max-Flow to other nodes might remain undetermined for most pivot choices _p_ and through multiple recursion depths, resulting in no cuts for them.

Second, and even if the first issue is resolved, the pivot _p_ itself could be present in optimal vertex _uv_-separators. This means that even when the minimum _pu_-cut separates a pair _v,u_, it might do so in a sub-optimal way that must not include the pivot _p_ in _C<sub>u,v</sub>_, and we would not have any indication for it. Moreover, there might not be any pivot choice that is absent from all separators, making the situation worse. To address these issues, we first provide an overview of a Monte Carlo version of our algorithm, to be followed by the necessary changes to achieve a Las Vegas algorithm.

## Overcoming barriers in \[AKT20a\]: A Monte Carlo algorithm

Despite the issues mentioned, the underlying intuition is applicable in our setting, and the shared symmetry property turns out to be enough to recover an \(\tilde{O}(m^2)\) running time. Our algorithm uses a similar framework as in \[AKT20a\], which involves a node partition inspired by minimum cuts from a random pivot and recursion. However, we introduce reinforcements in the form of additional Max-Flow queries to address the issues described. The main challenge is to ensure that the total number of additional queries does not exceed \(\tilde{O}(m)\), thus maintaining the total time complexity of \(\hat{O}(m^2)\) using the almost linear time algorithm for Max-Flow \[CKL<sup>+</sup>22, vdBCP<sup>+</sup>23\], as required.

To address the first issue, we implement the following changes. When a uniformly random node \(p\in V'\) is selected, in addition to the Max-Flow calls to all nodes \(u\in V'\backslash\{p\}\), we also directly query the Max-Flow between every node _q_ in the separator _C<sub>p,u</sub>_, and _u_. Recall that in our setting, it holds that \(|C_{p,u}|\le d_G(u)\) where _d<sub>G</sub>(u_) is the degree of node _u_ in the input graph _G_, and therefore the total number of additional queries for \(V'\) is at most the sum of node degrees in \(V'\). Since the node sets \(V'\) in any depth of the recursion are disjoint, the total number of extra queries is \(\tilde{O}(m)\).

To address the second issue, it is important to note that node pairs with a large separator, that is where both nodes have high degrees, are the most problematic in this context. Therefore, we would like to adopt a similar high degree/low degree approach to the one taken previously in \[AKT20b, HLSW23\]; solving Max-Flow between all pairs of high degree nodes, and letting the "main" algorithm handle the remaining pairs.

However, there are a few challenges involved in doing so. First, simply querying all pairwise nodes of high degree is not sufficient for our needs. This is because our requirement is exceptionally<tbc>

strong: that a uniformly random pivot in _any_ instance \(V'\) has a good chance of not being in many vertex separators, even when \(|V'|\) is much smaller than _n_, or even \(\sqrt{m}\). To achieve this, we query the Max-Flow between pairs of high degree nodes in every instance, but with a very high degree threshold compared to \(|V'|\), which is \(\hat{t}\ge|V'|/\mathsf{polylog}(n)\). By analyzing the recursion tree _T_, and that instances \(V'\) in any single depth of _T_ are disjoint, we conclude that there cannot be more than \(\tilde{O}(m)\) such queries in a single depth of _T_.

The second challenge is in the correctness proof for any node pair _u,v_. Similar to \[AKT20a\], we would like to reason about the pivot choice _p_ in the instance separating _u_ and _v_. However, vertex separators in our case introduce a worrisome dependency, as it could be for some instances that the only nodes separating _u_ and _v_ as pivots are _u_, _v_, and nodes within their separator _C<sub>u,v</sub>_. In this case, a careful analysis is needed to prove that such node pairs are likely to be pushed together (i.e. not being separated) to a later stage. We do this by using a more global argument that is independent of the particular instance separating _u_ and _v_, described below.

On one hand, while \(|V'|\) is large compared to |_C<sub>u,v</sub>_|, there is a decent probability to pick pivots outside of _C<sub>u,v</sub>_. On the other hand, if \(|V'|\) becomes small enough while _u_ and _v_ are still together, then they would be queried as a pair of high degree nodes in \(V'\). This motivates the following analysis (see Figure 2). Consider the path _P_ from the root of _T_ to \(V'_u\), the highest recursion node in _T_ where \(|V'_u|\) is smaller than a threshold set to \(\tilde{O}(d_G(u))\), where we assume without loss of generality that \(d(u)\le d(v)\). We show that with constant probability, all pivot choices in instances along _P_ do not belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_. Assuming that this event occurs, we have two cases. If _v_ has survived all the way down to \(V'_u\), then _v_ and _u_’s high degrees compared to \(|V'_u|\) would cause the algorithm to query them directly as a pair at this stage. Otherwise, they got separated earlier _along P_, and consequently, the pivot chosen at the moment of separation does not belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_.

## Converting to Las Vegas

The algorithm above may, with non zero probability, produce erroneous answers. This occurs for a pair _u,v_ if the pivots separating _u_ and _v_ belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_ in all _O_(log_n_) repetitions (and the pair _u,v_ was not queried directly). A natural starting point to address this issue is to increase the number of repetitions to _x_ for some _x\>\>_log_n_, instead of just _O_(log_n_) as in the Monte Carlo algorithm. By doing so, we can argue that the Max-Flow values that are at most _x_ will be preserved by a global analysis claim _and verification_ that no pivot was chosen too many times in instances of size at least \(\tilde{\Omega}(x)\) (throughout all repetitions). As a result, a sufficient number of distinct pivots must have been chosen, ensuring that at least one of the pivots separating _u_ and _v_ does not belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_. This could make the basis of a correct Las Vegas algorithm; unfortunately, the running time becomes _xmT(m_), which is too high as _x_ is only bounded by _n_. However, the part responsible for this high running time is the reinforcement queries rather than the basic recursion, and so there is still a hope.

Indeed, in the Las Vegas algorithm we are more strategic in performing reinforcement queries. We would like to perform such queries only for pairs that were required in at least _x_ repetitions, thus bounding the total number of distinct queries throughout all repetitions by \(\tilde{O}(m)\). Accordingly, we would claim that if a pair _u,v_ was _not_ required in at least _x_ repetitions (and thus was not queried directly) then it is surely separated many times, and so by many distinct pivots, in the basic recursion structure. Similar to before, this ensures that at least one of those pivots must not belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_, making the corresponding answer correct. However, even this only brings the total running time to _xnT(m_) which equals _n_<sup>2</sup>_m_ in the worst case. To further speed up the algorithm, we operate in stages focusing on a range \[_k,_2_k_) of Max-Flow values each time, thus incurring a factor _O_(log_n_) to the running time. Consequently, the relevant nodes, i.e, _terminals_, in each \[_k,_2_k_) stage are the nodes whose degrees are at least _k_, totaling at most _m/k_ nodes. At the same time, the minimum instance size we need to consider, as well as the number of repetitions required to ensure a sufficiently high number of distinct pivots for the terminals at this stage, is only \(\tilde{O}(k)\). This brings the total running time to \(\tilde{O}(m\cdot T(m))\), as required.

Note that unlike properties (\*) and (\*\*) detailed above, no local property can naturally be described in the Las Vegas version of our algorithm. However, a more global property is appropriate:

(\*\*\*) For every pair \(s',t'\) such that Max-Flow\((s',t')\in[k,2k)\), when the algorithm terminates at least one of the following holds in the \[_k,_2_k_) stage.<tbc>

1. \(s'\in S_{i,p}\) and \(t'\in C_{p,i}\), or \(s'\in C_{p,j}\) and \(t'\in S_{j,p}\), in at least _k_ repetitions for some _i_’s and _j_’s.<tbc>

2. \(s',t'\) are together in final instances of at least _k_ repetitions.<tbc>

3. (_S<sub>p,i</sub>,C<sub>p,i</sub>,S<sub>i,p</sub>_) in at least one of the repetitions corresponds to a minimum \(s't'\)-cut in _G_.

## 1.3.2 Nondeterministic algorithms

Several papers \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16, AKT20b, Li21\] have proposed nondeterministic algorithms as a means to restrict the applicability of SETH for conditional lower bounds. This method was introduced by Carmosino et al. \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16\], who also demonstrated that several problems, including APSP and 3SUM, are unlikely to have conditional lower bounds under SETH, assuming that NSETH holds.

## A related nondeterministic algorithm in [AKT20b].

Abboud et al. [AKT20b] presented a nondeterministic algorithm for the Gomory-Hu tree problem and used the framework of [CGI<sup>+</sup>16] to demonstrate that it is unlikely for this problem to have a super-linear SETH-based conditional lower bound. In their work, the nondeterministic algorithm simulates the Gomory-Hu algorithm [GH61] on a given input graph. Instead of using Max-Flow routines like in the Gomory-Hu algorithm, [AKT20b] employs a new accelerated operation that is equivalent to determining the maximum _pv_-flows from a guessed pivot _p_ to multiple other nodes _v_ simultaneously.

To quickly verify these multiple maximum flows, they used succinct data structures that exist for their setting of undirected graphs with edge-capacities (i.e. they used a cut-equivalent tree to verify cuts and a tree packing to verify flows). By applying the min-cut max-flow theorem [FF56], they concluded that if equality was established for each pair of guessed pivot _p_ and a corresponding node _v_, then the maximum flow guesses were correct. Consequently, the correctness of the simulation follows from the correctness of the Gomory-Hu algorithm.

## Obstacles in accelerating current algorithms.

In contrast, for hard variants even in unit (node or edge) capacities settings, existing algorithms [CLL13, HLSW23] have significant barriers to getting accelerated using nondeterminism. In the \(O(m^\omega)\) time algorithm for directed graphs with unit edge-capacities [CLL13], merely writing down (as opposed to finding) an inherent part of the algorithm - an inverted _m_ by _m_ matrix - takes _m_<sup>2</sup> time. Another algorithm, proposed for undirected graphs with unit node-capacities [HLSW23], utilizes an element-connectivity Gomory-Hu tree for nodes with smaller degrees and directly calls Max-Flow for node pairs with high degrees. However, in the case of dense graphs, this algorithm performs similarly to the naive approach of computing Max-Flow for every node pair. Moreover, even if element-connectivity Gomory-Hu trees can be found nondeterministically in linear time, the nondeterministic time complexity of All-Pairs Max-Flow in our setting would still be _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) due to a blow-up caused by set sampling techniques [IN12, PSY22, HLSW23] which seem necessary for element-connectivity based algorithms. As a result, alternative approaches are needed.

Let us focus on undirected graphs with unit node-capacities. Straightforward cut and flow witnesses for all pairs have a total size of _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) <sup>15</sup>, and verifying the flows could be done easily within a similar time since a flow here is composed of internally node-disjoint paths. However, verifying the cuts seems more challenging as it requires reading all edges to ensure that for each guess cut, no edges exist between the two separated parts<sup>16</sup>, and it is not immediately apparent how to perform this task faster than the naive approach.

A natural attempt to verify the cuts could be to use connectivity oracles to test whether pairs _u,v_ are still connected after removing their guessed separator. However, this approach might not be promising either, as conditional lower bounds are known for similar problems, such as the _d_-vertex- failure connectivity and even the vertex-failure global connectivity oracle [LS22].

## Our approach.

We enter all of the guessed cuts into a large binary matrix of size \(n^2\times n\), and then multiply it by the incidence matrix of the input graph. The resulting matrix enables us to confirm that there are no edges between the two parts in any of the guessed cuts, indicating that they are all valid vertex-cuts. This process takes the time of rectangular matrix multiplication, that is \(n^{\omega(2,1,1)}\le O(n^{3.252})\) [GU18]. In fact, we consider a slightly more general version of this<tbc>

<sup>15</sup>Following previous results in similar contexts [CGI<sup>+</sup>16, AKT20b, Li21], verifying both cuts and flows is crucial (1) to rule out _Turing_ reductions, and (2) as (minimum-) cuts are simply necessary for some nondeterministic algorithms to work (e.g., see [AKT20b], and Theorem 1.3 here). <sup>16</sup>For ease of exposition, we assume that there is no edge directly connecting the corresponding pair. However, this assumption is not necessary in any of our results.

approach, in two ways. First, it can be used with any algorithm for All-Pairs Max-Flow, not just the naive approach. This is beneficial for algorithms that require fewer than _n_<sup>2</sup> queries to Max-Flow on the input graph. Second, our approach can work with any data structure for All-Pairs Max- Flow, rather than just the trivial one that outputs all _n_<sup>2</sup> values. This expands the set of potential algorithms to include those outputting data structures whose size is smaller than the output size of All-Pairs Max-Flow, which is _n_<sup>2</sup>. Moreover, this approach is robust enough to work even on directed graphs with general edge-capacities. Therefore, for subquartic algorithms it essentially settles the nondeterministic time complexity of verifying the cuts in all variants of All-Pairs Max-Flow via folklore reductions with little overhead.

Regarding flows, the _O(n_) bound naturally applies only for unit node-capacities. Are there nontrivial upper bounds in other settings? For general node-capacities, we answer this question affirmatively! Specifically, we show that for graphs with general node-capacities, even directed, _O(n_) edges are always sufficient to ship the maximum _st_-flow. This is done by identifying a certain pattern that can be eliminated from any flow while still preserving its value and without violating the flow constraints or increasing the volume <sup>17</sup>. For directed (multi-) graphs with unit _edge_-capacities, we use the upper bound of \(n\sqrt{\mathbf{value}(f_{st})}\) proved in \[KL98\] for the volume of _st_-flows _f<sub>st</sub>_, where **value**(_f<sub>st</sub>_) represents the amount of flow shipped from _s_ to _t_ in _f<sub>st</sub>_. Using these flow bounds, a nondeterministic algorithm for each variant can guess succinct maximum flows for the queried pairs whose support is bounded by the corresponding upper bounds, and then verify their feasibility and values. Finally, we believe that our results may also be relevant in other related fields.

## 1.4 Preliminaries

### General notations.

• (_Miscellaneous._) Throughout, we only consider connected graphs with \(m\ge n-1\), and we use the terms "node" and "vertex" interchangeably. Let _G_=(_V,E,c_) be a graph with capacity function _c_ defined on either its edges or nodes. For positive integers _a,b_, and _c_, we denote by \(\omega(a,b,c)\) the exponent such that \(n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\) is the time it takes to multiply an \(n^a\times n^b\) matrix by an \(n^b\times n^c\) matrix.<tbc>

• (_Flows._) For an _st_-flow _f<sub>st</sub>_ in _G_, we use **volume**(_f<sub>st</sub>_) to denote the size of the support of _f<sub>st</sub>_ in _G_, which is simply the number of edges in _G_ with nonzero flow shipped by _f<sub>st</sub>_. We use **value**(_f<sub>st</sub>_) to denote the total flow value shipped from _s_ to _t_ in _f<sub>st</sub>_, that is the (capacity of) the out-degree minus the in-degree of _s_ (equivalently, the in-degree minus the out-degree of _t_) in _f<sub>st</sub>_. We may assume without loss of generality that _f<sub>st</sub>_ is acyclic (in particular, the in-degree of _s_ and the out-degree of _t_ is 0), as removing cycles in _f<sub>st</sub>_ does not change **value**(_f<sub>st</sub>_), which we typically attempt to maximize, and can only decrease **volume**(_f<sub>st</sub>_), which we typically attempt to minimize. We denote by _V(f<sub>st</sub>_) the set of nodes in the support of _f<sub>st</sub>_, i.e., nodes with adjacent edges carrying non-zero flow. Depending on the context, we may use _f<sub>st</sub>_ to denote the support of the corresponding flow.<tbc>

• (_Cuts._) Given two node sets \(A,B\subseteq V\) (which could also be a singletons), we use _E(A,B_) to denote the set of edges between _A_ and _B_, and **value**(_A,B_) to denote the capacity of edges between _A_ and _B_, i.e., \(\mathbf{value}(A,B)=\mathbf{value}(E(A,B))=\sum_{a\in A,b\in B}c(a,b)\). An edge _uv_-cut is denoted by (_S<sub>u,v</sub>,S<sub>v,u</sub>_), and a vertex _uv_-cut by (_S<sub>u,v</sub>,C<sub>u,v</sub>,S<sub>v,u</sub>_), where _C<sub>u,v</sub>_ is called a (vertex) _uv_-separator. In these contexts, **value**(_C<sub>u,v</sub>_) is defined as the capacity of the separator, given by \(\sum_{w\in C_{u,v}}c(w)\).<tbc>

<sup>17</sup>An alternative proof uses linear programming arguments \[Che24\], as discussed later in this paper.

• (_Max-Flow._) We use the notation Max-Flow_<sub>G</sub>(s,t_) for the minimum _st_-cut, or Min-Cut for short, in _G_. Depending on the context, this could either be the actual value or a query to an algorithm for computing it. In some cases, we may omit the graph _G_ subscript or the input (_s,t_) if it is clear from the context.

### Min-Cut data structure.

Following notations from \[AKT20a\], a _Min-Cut data structure_ for a graph family F is a data structure that given a graph \(G\in\mathcal{F}\), after a preprocessing phase which makes _t<sub>pq</sub>(m_) Max-Flow calls on _G_ and spends _t<sub>po</sub>(m_) time outside of these calls, can answer Min-Cut queries for any two nodes \(s,t\in V\) in amortized query time (or output sensitive time) _t<sub>mc</sub>(k<sub>st</sub>_), where _k<sub>st</sub>_ denotes the output size (number of edges or nodes in the output cut or separator). In particular, it means that the preprocessing time is at most \(t_{pq}(m)\cdot\hat{O}(m)+t_{po}(m)\) using \[CKL<sup>+</sup>22, vdBCP<sup>+</sup>23\], and the query time is \(O(k_{st}\cdot t_{mc}(k_{st}))\). We may also be interested in Min-Cut data structures that support queries of Max-Flow values instead of cuts, and we denote their query time by _t<sub>mf</sub>(m_).

### Non-reducibility.

Using notations from \[AKT20b\], a search problem _P_ is a binary relation, and we say that _S_ is a solution to instance _x_ iff \((x,S)\in P\). Let \(\mathrm{SOL}(x)=\{S:(x,S)\in P\}\) denote the set of solutions for instance _x_. We say that _P_ is a _total function_ if every instance _x_ has at least one solution, i.e. \(\mathrm{SOL}(x)\neq\emptyset\). Let \(\perp\) be the "don’t know" symbol and assume \(\perp\notin\mathrm{SOL}(x)\) for all _x_. In particular, in our context of Min-Cut data structures, _x_ is a graph, and SOL(_x_) is the set of all Min-Cut data structures with \(t_{mc}(m)=\hat{O}(1)\) for _x_ where _m_ is the number of edges in _x_. Next, we define the nondeterministic complexity of a total function.

**Definition 1.8** (Definition 3.1 from \[AKT20b\]. See also \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16\])**.** _We say that a total function P has nondeterministic time complexity T(n_) _if there is a deterministic Turing Machine M such that for every instance x of P with size_ |_x_|=_n:_

a. \(\forall g,\mathsf{DTIME}(M(x,g))\le T(n)\)_, i.e., the time complexity of M is bounded by T(n);_<tbc>

b. \(\exists g,M(x,g)\in\mathrm{SOL}(x)\)_, i.e., at least one guess leads M to output a solution;_<tbc>

c. \(\forall g,M(x,g)\in\{\perp\}\cup\mathrm{SOL}(x)\)_, i.e., every guess leads M to output either a solution or "don’t know"._

The following is a definition of (deterministic) fine-grained reductions from a decision problem to a total function. These are Turing reductions.

**Definition 1.9** (Definition 3.12 from \[AKT20b\]. See also \[Wil18\])**.** _Let L be a language and P be a total function, and let_ \(T_L(\cdot)\) _and_ \(T_P(\cdot)\) _be time bounds. We say that_ (_L,T<sub>L</sub>_) _admits a fine-grained reduction to_ (_P,T<sub>P</sub>_) _if for all_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _there is a_ \(\gamma>0\) _and a deterministic Turing machine M<sup>P</sup> (with an access to an oracle that generates a solution to every instance of P) such that:_

1. _M<sup>P</sup> decides L correctly on all inputs when given a correct oracle for P._<tbc>

_2._ _Let_ \(\tilde{Q}(M^P,x)\) _denote the set of oracle queries made by M<sup>P</sup> on input x of length n. Then the query lengths obey the bound_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\forall x,\mathsf{DTIME}(M^P,|x|)+\sum_{q\in\tilde{Q}(M,x)}(T_P(|q|))^{1-\varepsilon}\le(T_L(n))^{1-\gamma}.\)<tbc>

<tbc>Theorem 3.13 in \[AKT20b\], provided below, further showed a non-reducibility result under NSETH for total functions with small nondeterministic complexity.

**Theorem 1.10.** _Suppose P is a total function with nondeterministic time complexity T(m). If for some_ \(\delta>0\)_, there is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from k-SAT with time-bound_ 2_<sup>n</sup> to P with time bound_ \(T(m)^{1+\delta}\)_, i.e. from_ (_k-SAT,_2_<sup>n</sup>_) _to_ \((P,T(m)^{1+\delta})\) _then NSETH is false._

### Non-reducibility for deterministic vs. randomized reductions.

Our results, along with the framework for non-reducibility in \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16\], do not address the possibility of proving lower bounds based on SETH using a randomized fine-grained reduction. The reason is that NSETH, upon which this framework is built, does not remain plausible when facing randomization (see \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16, Wil16\]). That said, we are not aware of any instances where this barrier has been successfully bypassed with randomization. Furthermore, one can use a non-uniform variant of NSETH called NUNSETH, under which our results also hold for randomized reductions with bounded error.

## 2 Non-Reducibility Results

In the absence of _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bounds for general algorithms for All-Pairs Max-Flow, it may be tempting to utilize the commonly used SETH as a hardness assumption, and design a reduction from SAT to prove that the problem requires a running time of _n_<sup>4-_o_(1)</sup>. However, we demonstrate here that in most settings of the problem, such (deterministic) reductions are not possible under NSETH, thus proving our Theorems 1.3, 1.5, and 1.6. Technically, our main results in this section are fast _nondeterministic_ algorithms for solving All-Pairs Max-Flow in various settings. In fact, our nondeterministic framework is even more general, as it is applicable to Min-Cut data structures. This could be significant because in some settings, a data structure for All-Pairs Max-Flow could potentially be much smaller than _n_<sup>2</sup> - similar to cut-equivalent trees in the case of undirected graphs with edge capacities, and we aim to capture these scenarios as well with our framework.

Then, we reach our non-reducibility conclusions under NSETH by an argument first made in \[CGI<sup>+</sup>16\] to rule out SETH-based reductions to various problems, including 3SUM and All- Pairs Shortest-Path. The argument was later rewritten \[AKT20b\] to adapt from decision problems or functions (where each input has exactly one output) to total functions as every graph has at least one Gomory-Hu tree, which was the focus of \[AKT20b\]. This adaptation is detailed in Section 1.4, with Theorem 1.10. We use the same total function definition more generally for any Min-Cut data structure with \(t_{mc}=\hat{O}(1)\), which is a total function since every graph has at least one such data structure: just compute the _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) cuts naively in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_m_) time (so in this case, _t<sub>pq</sub>(m),t<sub>po</sub>(m_)=_n_<sup>2</sup>). Next is our main framework, which is central to achieving our nondeterministic algorithms across all settings.

**Theorem 2.1.** _Suppose there is a Min-Cut data structure_ D _that given a graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{F}\) _on m edges and n nodes, after a preprocessing phase which, with high probability, makes t<sub>pq</sub>(m_) _Max-Flow calls on G and spends t<sub>po</sub>(m_) _time outside of these calls, can answer queries correctly in t<sub>mc</sub>(m_) _output sensitive time._

_Then, the nondeterministic time complexity for constructing a Min-Cut data structure for G is_ \(\tilde{t}_p(m)=O(t_{po}(m)+n^{\omega(log_n(|Q|),1,1)}+\sum_{(u,v)\in Q}volume(f_{uv}))\) _with_ \(\tilde{t}_{mc}(m)=t_{mc}(m)\)_, where_ \(Q\subseteq V\times V\) _is the set of pairs for which the t<sub>pq</sub>(m_) _Max-Flow calls are made, and f<sub>uv</sub> is any maximum uv-flow in G._

The main idea in the proof of Theorem 2.1 is to first verify all the minimum cuts that D will use on _G_ in hindsight. Then, we simulate D and whenever we encounter a Max-Flow query, we assert the corresponding guess. The correctness follows immediately from the correctness of D. Before proving Theorem 2.1, we state a technical lemma regarding the nondeterministic time it takes to verify maximum flows for a given set of node pairs _Q_.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Given a set of node pairs_ \(Q\subseteq V\times V\)_, the nondeterministic complexity of solving Max-Flow for all_ \((u,v)\in Q\) _is_ \(O\left(n^{\omega(\mathrm{log}_n(|Q|),1,1)}+\sum_{(u,v)\in Q}\mathbf{volume}(f_{uv})\right)\).

_Proof of Theorem 2.1._ A nondeterministic algorithm first guesses the random bits of D (if D is randomized Las Vegas) and a set of node pairs to be queried _Q_. It then solves _Q_ nondeterministically using Lemma 2.2. Finally, it simulates D (on a deterministic Turing machine) with the guessed random bits, and whenever encountering a Max-Flow query, it asserts the validity of the corresponding stored answer for the node pair. By Lemma 2.2, verifying the Max-Flow for _Q_ takes a total time of \(O\left(n^{\omega(\mathrm{log}_n(|Q|),1,1)}+\sum_{(u,v)\in Q}\mathbf{volume}(f_{uv})\right)\), and otherwise (for some guess) the total running time is bounded by _t<sub>po</sub>(m_). The correctness follows immediately from the correctness of D, and so the proof of Theorem 2.1 is concluded.

_Proof of Lemma 2.2._ First, guess a list \(\{p_{uv}\}_{(u,v)\in Q}\) for the node pairs in _Q_. We want to verify quickly two things for each pair (_u,v_):

1. that there exists a _uv_-flow _f<sub>uv</sub>_ such that \(\mathbf{value}(f_{uv})\ge p_{uv}\), and<tbc>

2. that there exists a _uv_-cut (_S<sub>uv</sub>,T<sub>uv</sub>_) such that \(\mathbf{value}(S_{uv},T_{uv})\le p_{uv}\).

By the min-cut max-flow theorem \[FF56\], it would imply that the guessed _p<sub>uv</sub>_’s are maximum _uv_-flow values. But how can we verify these conditions quickly? Verifying the cut or flow values explicitly for each pair would be too costly, as it might take at least _m_ time using a straightforward approach. Thus, the total time would be \(O(|Q|\cdot m)\), which does not provide any significant advantage to nondeterminism. Therefore, we need to employ a more careful strategy.

## Verifying lower bounds.

For the flow lower bounds, verifying the guessed values \(\{p_{uv}\}_{(u,v)\in Q}\) in the proper time of \(\sum_{(u,v)\in Q}\mathbf{volume}(f_{uv})\) is simple; just guess succinct flows _f<sub>uv</sub>_ for all pairs \((u,v)\in Q\), and then verify their validity and values _p<sub>uv</sub>_, i.e., that the flow conservation and capacity constraints hold, and that \(\mathbf{value}(f_{uv})\ge p_{uv}\). If any verification step returned "no", reject, otherwise accept. The verification time per flow is proportional to the number of edges in its support, that is _O_(**volume**(_f<sub>uv</sub>_)), as required.

As a side note, the challenge in making this part of Lemma 2.2 useful will be to show for any maximum _uv_-flow _f<sub>uv</sub>_ that _there exists_ a (perhaps alternative) succinct flow \(f'_{uv}\) shipping the same amount of flow in _G_ while keeping the flow constraints, or to find a proper algorithm with few calls to Max-Flow. This will be elaborated on in Section 2.1.

## Verifying upper bounds.

For the cut upper bounds, the proof is similar across all variants, and it can even be applied to directed graphs with general _edge_ capacities. Therefore, we will only present a proof for this particular variant, while noting that folklore reductions from the other variants are sufficient for our purposes.

Technically, the nondeterministic algorithm guesses a partition (_S<sub>uv</sub>,T<sub>uv</sub>=V_\\_S_) for every pair \((u,v)\in Q\), and then it utilizes fast matrix multiplication to simultaneously verify that the cut values are smaller than the guessed values \(\{p_{uv}\}_{(u,v)\in Q}\), i.e. it checks that for all \((u,v)\in Q\), it holds that \(\mathbf{value}(S_{uv},T_{uv})\le p_{uv}\). In more detail, we define a binary matrix \(P_{|Q|\times n}\), where the rows correspond to the pairs in _Q_ and the columns correspond to the nodes in the graph. In this matrix, the entry _P_\[_g<sub>uv</sub>,w_\] is set to 1 if \(w\in S_{uv}\), and to 0 otherwise, where _g<sub>uv</sub>_ is the index of the pair \((u,v)\in Q\) (by some arbitrary order). Lastly, let _M<sub>G</sub>_ be the incidence matrix of the graph _G_, where an entry _M<sub>G</sub>_\[_u,v_\] is the weight of the edge from _u_ to _v_ in _G_, and is 0 if no such edge exists. With these notations, we are now ready to describe the cuts verification algorithm.

**Algorithm: Cuts Verification**

1. perform the multiplication \(P'=PM_G\).<tbc>

2. for every pair \((u,v)\in Q\) verify that \(\sum_{z\in T_{uv}}P'[g_{uv},z]\le p_{uv}\).<tbc>

3. if at least one verification step returned "no", reject, otherwise accept.

### Correctness.

Observe that for every node _z_, \(P'[g_{uv},z]\) is precisely \(\sum_{w\in S_{uv}}c(w,z)\), and thus for each pair \((u,v)\in Q\), the verified values are precisely what we are looking for:

\(\sum_{z\in T_{uv}}P'[g_{uv},z]=\sum_{w\in S_{uv},z\in T_{uv}}c(w,z)=\mathbf{value}(S_{uv},T_{uv}).\)

### Running time.

The total size of |_Q_| cut guesses (by their nodes) is \(O(|Q|\cdot n)\). Multiplying an \(|Q|\times n\) matrix with an \(n\times n\) matrix takes \(n^{\omega(\mathrm{log}_n(|Q|),1,1)}\) time, and counting _O(n_) entries per pair of nodes in _Q_ takes \(O(|Q|\cdot n)\) time, which brings the total verification time to \(O\left(n^{\omega(\mathrm{log}_n(|Q|),1,1)}+|Q|\cdot n\right)\le O\left(n^{\omega(\mathrm{log}_n(|Q|),1,1)}\right)\), concluding Lemma 2.2.

## 2.1 Succinct _st_-flows in Various Settings

In this section, we detail the volume upper bounds for flows in various settings, that we either prove or reference.

### 2.1.1 Unit node-capacities

**Lemma 2.3.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be an undirected graph with unit node capacities,_ \(s,t\in V\) _a pair of nodes, and f<sub>st</sub> an st-flow in G. Then_ \(\mathbf{volume}(f_{st})\le 2n\).

_Proof._ Observe that _f<sub>st</sub>_ consists of internally node-disjoint paths. Therefore, each node in _V(f<sub>st</sub>_) except for _s_ and _t_, has degree 2 in _f<sub>st</sub>_, and consequently we have \(\mathbf{volume}(f_{st})\le 2n\), as required.

### 2.1.2 Unit edge-Capacities

In contrast to the case of unit node-capacities, here, nodes in _V(f<sub>st</sub>_) can have arbitrarily high degrees in _f<sub>st</sub>_, and it is not immediately evident that the total volume of _f<sub>st</sub>_ is bounded by anything significantly smaller than _m_. We use a general lemma from \[KL98\] that works even for arbitrary integer capacities, in our context of (multi-)graphs with unit edge-capacities:

**Lemma 2.4** (Theorem 7.1 in \[KL98\], rephrased)**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a directed graph with integer edge-capacities,_ \(s,t\in V\) _a pair of nodes, and f<sub>st</sub> an st-flow in G. Then_ \(\mathbf{volume}(f_{st})\le\tilde{O}\left(n\sqrt{\mathbf{value}(f_{st})}\right)\).

### 2.1.3 General node-capacities

We will now prove that the total volume necessary to ship any flow value in a node-capacitated network never exceeds 2_n_.

**Lemma 2.5.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a directed graph with node-capacities,_ \(s,t\in V\) _be a pair of nodes, and f<sub>st</sub> be an st-flow in G. Then there exists an st-flow_ \(f'_{st}\) _in G of the same value_ \(\mathbf{value}(f'_{st})=\mathbf{value}(f_{st})\) _such that_ \(\mathbf{volume}(f'_{st})\le 2n\).

The high-level idea of the proof is that any valid _st_-flow _f<sub>st</sub>_ can be transformed into a succinct _st_-flow \(f'_{st}\) by eliminating all copies of a certain pattern from _f<sub>st</sub>_, while preserving the flow value and meeting the flow constraints. The pattern that will be eliminated is called an _anti-directed closed walk_ (see Figure 3). It is, in our context, a directed graph whose underlying graph forms a _simple_ closed walk, that is where no edge appears twice, and consecutive edges have alternate directions, or in other words, no pair of consecutive edges forms a directed path. Note that an anti-directed closed walk must have an even number of edges.

**Definition 2.6** (anti-directed closed walk)**.** _For any integer_ \(\ell\)_, an_ anti-directed closed walk _is a simple closed walk_ \(C=(u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{2\ell})\) _where for each_ \(i\in[1,\dots,2\ell]\)_, the edges between u_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_,u<sub>i</sub> and between u<sub>i</sub>,u_<sub>_i_+1</sub> _are oriented in one of two ways: either (1) towards u<sub>i</sub>, that is_ \((u_{i-1},u_i),(u_{i+1},u_i)\in E(C)\)_, or (2) away from u<sub>i</sub>, that is_ \((u_i,u_{i-1}),(u_i,u_{i+1})\in E(C)\).

For an anti-directed closed walk _C_ we define _P<sub>out</sub>_ (respectively, _P<sub>in</sub>_) as the set of all node occurrences \(u_i\in C\) whose adjacent edges are oriented in way (1) (respectively, in way (2)). Note that |_P<sub>in</sub>_|=|_P<sub>out</sub>_|, \(P_{in}\cap P_{out}=\emptyset\), and \(P_{in}\cup P_{out}=C\).

The related concept of anti-directed _cycles_ has been studied before in other contexts, such as edge partitioning \[AHR81\] and the existence of anti-directed hamiltonian cycles \[DM15\]. We are now ready to prove Lemma 2.5.

## 3.1 Our Reinforced Tree-Like Data Structure: A Monte Carlo Version

In the remainder of this section, we demonstrate how to construct a data structure D that employs a tree structure to efficiently answer Max-Flow queries for an input graph _G_=(_V,E_). For a more conceptual grasp of the framework, we recommend the reader to become familiar with the original approximation algorithm designed for the edge-capacities case \[AKT20a\].

### Preprocessing

At a high level, the basic framework involves recursion. We begin by partitioning an instance \(V'\subseteq V\) using an _expansion_ operation into a few sets \(S_i\subseteq V'\), on which we will apply the operation recursively until they have a size of 1. This partition will (almost) satisfy property (\*\*) that was discussed in Section 1.3.1. To help us keep track of these partitions, we maintain a recursion-tree _T_. Each node \(t_{V^\prime}\) in the tree corresponds to an expansion operation, and stores \(V'\) along with some auxiliary information, such as a mapping from each node \(v\in V'\) to a cut (_S<sub>p,f(v)</sub>,C<sub>p,f(v)</sub>,S<sub>f(v),p</sub>_), as well as to other cuts computed directly for it. To perform a query on a pair \(u,v\in V\) we first check whether Max-Flow(_u,v_) was computed in one of the direct queries throughout the algorithm run. If not, we immediately gain information about the structure of the minimum vertex _uv_-cut. Then, we search for the recursion-node in _T_ that separated _u_ and _v_, i.e. the last \(V'\) that contains both _u_ and _v_, and output the smaller of (at most) two cuts stored in that node.

We will now shift our focus to the recursion tree and later prove that its depth is bounded by _O_(log_n_). At each depth of the tree, expansion operations are executed on disjoint subsets \(V'\). This is crucial for bounding the total number of Max-Flow queries involved in the expansion operations at that depth, which we will show is at most \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\). More precisely, we run this algorithm _O_(log_n_) times on \(V'=V\) , thus constructing _O_(log_n_) recursion trees and demonstrate that with high probability, for every _u,v_ query the correct answer can be obtained from at least one of the recursion trees.

The following is the expansion operation on a subset \(V'\subseteq V\) . If \(V'=V\) (i.e., in the beginning) then repeat 4log_n_ times.

1. let \(V'_H:=\{u\in V':\alpha(u)\ge|V'|/20log_{4/3}n\}\), and compute directly Max-Flow(_u,v_) for every pair of nodes \(u,v\in V'_H\).<tbc>

2. pick a pivot node \(p\in V'\) uniformly at random.<tbc>

3. for every node \(u\in V'\backslash\{p\}\) perform a query Max-Flow(_p,u_) to get a vertex-cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,C<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_) where \(p\in S_{p,u}\), \(u\in S_{u,p}\), and the vertex-cut separating _u_ and _v_ (i.e. a _uv_-separator) is _C<sub>p,u</sub>_. Then, compute the intersection with \(V'\) of the side of _u_ in the cut, that is \(S_{u,p}\cap V'\), and denote this set by \(S'_{u,p}\), and similarly define \(S'_{p,u}\) and \(C'_{p,u}\).<tbc>

4. the following is a _reassignment_ process, which is designed for our case of vertex-cuts. We aim to satisfy three main criteria when reassigning nodes to cuts.<tbc>

(a) we may only assign a node _v_ to a cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,C<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_) with the same value as **value**(_C<sub>p,v</sub>_), which is an optimal cut for _v_. This is necessary to eventually output optimal cuts.<tbc>

(b) we prioritize assigning _v_ to an optimal _pu_-cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,C<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_) that separates _v_ from _p_ and has a _small cardinality_ \(|S'_{u,p}|\). This ensures that the sets significantly decrease in size with each recursive step and thus upper bounds the total recursion depth by _O_(log_n_).<tbc>

(c) we can only assign two nodes _u,v_ to different sets if we have evidence for doing so in the form of a (likely optimal) vertex-cut _C_ that separates one but not the other from _p_, and thus separates them.<tbc>

<tbc>Satisfying all of the above criteria at the same time requires the following process. We define a reassignment function \(f:V'\rightarrow V'\cup\{\perp\}\) such that for every node \(u\in V'\backslash\{p\}\) with cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,C<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_), we reassign _u_ to _v_, denoted _f(u_)=_v_ with the cut (_S<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>_,C<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>_,S<sub>f(u),p</sub>_) as follows. Denote by \(V_{small},V'_{small}\) two initially identical sets, each containing all nodes _u_ such that \(|S'_{u,p}|\le n'/2\), and denote by \(V_{big},V'_{big}\) two sets, both are initially equal to \(V'\backslash V_{small}\).<tbc>

<tbc>Sort _V<sub>small</sub>_ by Max-Flow(_p,u_), and for all \(u\in V_{small}\) from low Max-Flow(_p,u_) to high and for every node \(v\in S'_{u,p}\cap V'_{small}\), set _f(v_)=_u_ and then remove _v_ from \(V'_{small}\). Furthermore, for every node \(v\in S'_{u,p}\cap V'_{big}\), if Max-Flow(_p,u_)=Max-Flow(_p,v_) then set _f(v_)=_u_ and then remove _v_ from \(V'_{big}\). Finally, set \(f(v)=\perp\) for every node _v_ for which _f_ was not assigned a value (including _p_).<tbc>

<tbc>To get the partition, let _IM(f_) be the image of _f_ (excluding \(\perp\)) and for each \(i\in IM(f)\) let _f_<sup>-1</sup>(_i_) be the set of all nodes _u_ that were reassigned by _f_ to the cut (_S<sub>p,f(i_)</sub>_,C<sub>p,f(i_)</sub>_,S<sub>f(i),p</sub>_). Notice that the nodes in \(V'_{big}\), which include _p_, were not assigned to any set. Thus, we get the partition of \(V'\) into \(V'_{big}\) and each set in \(\{f^{-1}(i)\}_{i\in IM(f)}\). The latter sets may satisfy property (\*\*), but \(V'_{big}\) may not; in particular, (\*\*).3 could be violated because \(V'_{big}\) does not correspond to a minimum cut, and therefore it will be handled separately shortly.<tbc>

5. if |_V<sub>small</sub>|\<n/_4 then _p_ is a failed pivot. In this situation, re-start the expansion operation at step 1 and continue choosing new pivots until \(|V_{small}|\ge n/4\), or until the number of repetitions is more than 4log_n_, in which case output "failure". We show that the latter occurs with low probability.<tbc>

6. for every \(u\in V'\backslash\{p\}\) and \(q\in C_{p,f(u)}\), query directly Max-Flow(_q,u_).<tbc>

7. finally, we recursively compute the expansion operation on each of the sets of the partition, while their sizes are bigger than 1. Let us describe what we store at the recursion node \(t_{V^\prime}\) corresponding to the just-completed expansion operation on \(V'\) with pivot _p_. We store \((|V'|-1)+\alpha(V')\) cuts in \(t_{V^\prime}\), including:<tbc>

(a) for each \(u,v\in V'_H\) we store _C<sub>u,v</sub>_.<tbc>

(b) for each node \(u_{big}\in V'_{big}\backslash\{p\}\) we store the cut (_S<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,C<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,S<sub>u<sub>big</sub>,p</sub>_).<tbc>

(c) for each node _u_ in one of the other sets of the partition \(\{f^{-1}(i)\}_{i\in IM(f)}\) we store the cut it was reassigned to (_S<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>_,C<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>,S<sub>f(u),p</sub>_).<tbc>

(d) for each \(u\in V'\) and \(q\in C_{p,f(u)}\) we store _C<sub>q,u</sub>_.<tbc>

<tbc>We also keep an array of pointers from each node to its corresponding cuts and also their values, and we call this array _A_. We also store, for each node of \(V'\), the name of the set in the partition that it belongs to, in an array _B_.<tbc>

## Queries

To answer a query for a pair of nodes _u_ and _v_, we first check if Max-Flow(_u,v_) was computed directly for them. If so, we output the corresponding separator. Otherwise, we do the following for each recursion tree _T_ and pick the answer with minimal value: we go to the recursion depth that separated _u_ and _v_, which corresponds to some node \(t_{V^\prime}\) in _T_, and output a pointer to one of the two corresponding cuts (_S<sub>p,f(u)</sub>,C<sub>p,f(u)</sub>,S<sub>f(u),p</sub>_) or (_S<sub>p,f(v)</sub>,C<sub>p,f(v)</sub>,S<sub>f(v),p</sub>_) - the one with smaller capacity among the (at most) two that separate _u_ and _v_. We prove that at least one of the two cuts separates them. To find out which recursive node separates _u_ and _v_, we start from the root and continue down, guided by the array _B_, to the nodes that contain both _u_ and _v_ until we reach a node that separates them. The query time depends on the depth of the recursion, which we will show later to be logarithmic for all trees.

The claim below proves that the cut returned for each pair _u,v_ is optimal with high probability. The main idea is that either both \(\alpha(u)\) and \(\alpha(v)\) are high with respect to \(n':=|V'|\) in the instance \(V'\) that separates them, in which case the algorithm computes Max-Flow(_u,v_) directly, or at least one of \(\alpha(u)\) and \(\alpha(v)\) is small, in which case their separator is small, and _p_ is unlikely to be in it. Then, assume without loss of generality that \(\text{Max-Flow}(p,u)\le\text{Max-Flow}(p,v)\). Consequently, either _C<sub>p,u</sub>_ is optimal for Max-Flow(_u,v_), or \(v\in C_{p,u}\), and we computed Max-Flow(_u,v_) directly. More formally,
