Indeed, (_S_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,S_<sub>_f(u),p_</sub>) is the cut returned.<tbc>

(b) Otherwise,<tbc>

<tbc>Max-Flow(_p,u_)=Max-Flow(_p,v)._<tbc>

<tbc>First, we see that \(v\notin S'_{f(u),p}\). Otherwise, as \(u,v\in V_{small}\) they must have been sent to the same recursion instance, contradicting our assumption on the expansion operation on \(V'\). Like before, it implies that Max-Flow(_u,v_)=Max-Flow(_p,u_), and so for this pivot the algorithm can output (_S_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,S_<sub>_f(u),p_</sub>) as the optimal cut for _u,v_, as required.<tbc>

2. Second, we consider the case when one of the nodes is in \(V'_{big}\) and the other is in \(V'_{small}\), and we separate into three sub-cases according to their Max-Flow value to _p_. More specifically, let \(u_{big}\in V'_{big}\) and \(u\notin V'_{big}\) be nodes where the minimum cut (_S_<sub>_p,u<sub>big</sub>_</sub>_,C_<sub>_p,u<sub>big</sub>_</sub>_,S_<sub>_u<sub>big</sub>,p_</sub>) is the cut corresponding to _u<sub>big</sub>_.<tbc>

(a) If<tbc>

<tbc>Max-Flow(_p,u<sub>big</sub>)\>_Max-Flow(_p,f(u_)),<tbc>

<tbc>then \(u_{big}\notin S'_{f(u),p}\) as otherwise _u<sub>big</sub>_ would have been assigned to _f(u_), as _f(u_) is in _V<sub>small</sub>_. Together with 3.2, we have that \(u_{big}\in S'_{p,f(u)}\). We conclude that (_S_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_S_<sub>_f(u),p_</sub>) is a minimum _u<sub>big</sub>v_-cut.<tbc>

(b) If<tbc>

<tbc>Max-Flow(_p,u<sub>big</sub>_)=Max-Flow(_p,f(u_)),<tbc>

<tbc>then it must be that \(u_{big}\notin S'_{f(u),p}\), since otherwise, as \(u_{big}\in V'_{big}\) and when the algo rithm examined _f(u_) it did not set _f(u<sub>big</sub>_):=_f(u_), it must have been the case for a node _x_ that was either _f(u_) or before _f(u_) in the order (i.e. such that \(\text{\textbf{value}}(C_{p,x})\le\text{\textbf{value}}(C_{p,f(u)}))\) that _u<sub>big</sub>_ was tested for the first time, with **value**(_C<sub>p,x</sub>)\>_**value**(_C_<sub>_p,u<sub>big</sub>_</sub>), and so **value**(_C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>)_\>_**value**(_C_<sub>_p,u<sub>big</sub>_</sub>). However, by our assumption it holds that **value**(_C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>)=**value**(_C_<sub>_p,u<sub>big</sub>_</sub>), in contradiction. Together with 3.2 we get \(u_{big}\in S'_{p,f(v)}\), and like before, the returned cut (_S_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,C_<sub>_p,f(u_)</sub>_,S_<sub>_f(u),p_</sub>) is optimal for _u<sub>big</sub>,u_.<tbc>

(c) Finally, if<tbc>

<tbc>Max-Flow(_p,u<sub>big</sub>)\<_Max-Flow(_p,f(u_)),<tbc>

<tbc>then (_S<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,C<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,S<sub>u<sub>big</sub>,p</sub>_) separates _u<sub>big</sub>_ and _u_, and with 3.2 and 3.1 providing an optimal minimum cut, concluding the claim.

## Running time

Here, we prove the upper bounds on the preprocessing time, by proving that with high probability, the algorithm terminates after \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\) calls to Max-Flow and \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)n)\) time outside of these calls.

At a high level, our aim is to bound the size of each of the sets in the partition in an expansion operation by \(3|V'|/4\), which implies a bound of _O_(log_n_) on the height of the recursion tree. This bound is immediate for the sets {_f_<sup>-1</sup>(_i_)}_<sub>i</sub>_ since they are subsets of cuts _S<sub>u,p</sub>_ of nodes _u_ in _V<sub>small</sub>_ and, by definition, satisfy that \(|S'_{u,p}|\le n'/2\). Therefore, we only need to worry about \(V'_{big}\). However, any node _u_ that is initially in _V<sub>small</sub>_ will end up reassigned to one of the sets {_f_<sup>-1</sup>(_i_)}_<sub>i</sub>_ and not to \(V'_{big}\). Thus, it suffices to argue that \(|V_{small}|\ge|V'|/4\). To this end, we cite a lemma from \[AKT20a\] which shows that for a randomly chosen _p_, at least 1/4 of the nodes \(u\in V'\) satisfy that the side of _u_ is smaller than the side of _p_, and so they will end up in _V<sub>small</sub>_. We provide a more formal proof of this below, starting with a general lemma about tournaments.

**Lemma 3.4** (Lemma 2.4 in \[AKT20a\])**.** _Let Y_=(_V<sub>Y</sub>,E<sub>Y</sub>_) _be a directed graph on n nodes and m edges that contains a tournament on V<sub>Y</sub>. Then Y contains at least n/_2 _nodes with an out-degree at least n/_4.

The following is a corollary of Lemma 3.4 concerning cuts between every pair of nodes, and it is an adaptation of Corollary 2.5 in \[AKT20a\] to vertex-cuts.

**Corollary 3.5.** _Let F_=(_V<sub>F</sub>,E<sub>F</sub>_) _be a graph where each pair of nodes_ \(u,v\in V_F\) _is associated with a cut_ (_S<sub>u,v</sub>,C<sub>u,v</sub>,S<sub>v,u</sub>_) _where_ \(u\in S_{u,v},v\in S_{v,u}\) _(possibly more than one pair of nodes are associated with each cut), and let_ \(V'_F\subseteq V_F\)_. Then there exist_ \(|V'_F|/2\) _nodes_ \(p'\) _in_ \(V'_F\) _such that at least_ \(|V'_F|/4\) _of the other nodes_ \(w\in V'_F\backslash\{p'\}\) _satisfy_ \(|S_{p^\prime,w}\cap V'_F|\ge|S_{w,p^\prime}\cap V'_F|\).

_Proof._ Let \(H_F(V'_F)\) denote the _helper graph_ of _F_ on \(V'_F\), where there is a directed edge from \(u\in V'_F\) to \(v\in V'_F\) iff \(|S_{u,v}\cap V'_F|>|S_{v,u}\cap V'_F|\). By Lemma 3.4, since \(H_F(V'_F)\) contains a tournament on \(V'_F\), Corollary 3.5 holds.

Next, apply Corollary 3.5 on _G_, and let \(H=H_G(V')\) be the helper graph of _G_ on \(V'\) with the reassigned cuts. As a result, with probability at least 1/2, the pivot _p_ is one of the nodes with out-degree at least \(n'/4\). In that case, when the algorithm partitions \(V'\), it must be that \(\mathrm{max}_i|f^{-1}(i)|\le n'/4\), and \(|f^{-1}(\perp)|\le 3n'/4\), that is, the largest set created is of size at most \(3n'/4\). This is because, while the separated parts _S<sub>u,v</sub>_ and _S<sub>v,u</sub>_ for each _uv_-cut do not cover the entire node set as the case in \[AKT20a\], the condition \(|S_{p,v}\cap V'_F|\ge|S_{v,p}\cap V'_F|\) for adding an edge in the tournament still implies that \(|S_{f(v),p}\cap V'_F|\le n'/2\), meaning that _v_ remains in _V<sub>small</sub>_ after the reassignment process in our setting too.

After making _O(n_log_n_) successful pivot choices, the algorithm terminates with the total depth of the recursion tree being at most log<sub>4/3</sub>_n_. Note that in step 5, the algorithm verifies the choice of _p_ and only proceeds with a successful pivot choice. Therefore, it suffices to bound the running time of the algorithm given only successful pivot choices. The probability of having 4log_n_ consecutive failures in a single instance is bounded by (1/2)<sup>4log_n_</sup>=1_/n_<sup>4</sup>, and by applying the union bound over<tbc>

the total \(\tilde{O}(n)\) instances in all recursion trees, the probability of having at least one instance that takes more than 4log_n_ attempts until a successful choice of _p_ is bounded by 1_/n_<sup>2</sup>.

We now turn our attention to bounding the total number of Max-Flow queries. The total number of queries performed for pairs in step 1, i.e. where both nodes have degrees at least \(n'/(20log_{4/3}n)\), in a single instance \(V'\) is at most:

\(|V'_H|^2=|\{u\in V':\alpha(u)>|V'|/(20log_{4/3}n)\}|^2\le\sum_{u\in V'_H}\alpha(u)20log_{4/3}n\le\alpha(V'_H)\cdot 20log_{4/3}n.\)

The total number of queries performed in steps 3 and 6 in one instance \(V'\) is at most<tbc>

\(|V'|+\sum_{u\in V^\prime}\alpha(p,u)=|V'|+\alpha(V').\)

<tbc>Thus, the total number of queries performed in one depth _i_ is

\(\sum_{V^\prime\text{in depth}i}\left(\alpha(V'_H)\cdot 20log_{4/3}n+|V'|+\alpha(V')\right)\le\alpha(V)\cdot 20log_{4/3}n+n+\alpha(V)\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)),\)

and summing over all depths, repetitions, and trees, we get a total number of Max-Flow queries of \(t_{pq}(m)=\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\). Note that most of the time spent outside of Max-Flow calls is in steps 3 and 4, and it is bounded by _O(n_) per cut computed, thus a total of \(t_{po}(m)=\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)n)\), as required.

### Space usage

We aim to bound the total space used by the data structure, focusing on the more demanding steps and beginning with item 1 of Theorem 3.1.

• To bound the space occupied by cuts in both step 1 and step 6, we focus on a \[_k,_2_k_) range of separator sizes each time, incurring an _O_(log_n_) factor in the space bound. On one hand, at most \((\alpha(V)/k)^2\) node pairs can have separators with size in \[_k,_2_k_), and on the other hand, as demonstrated earlier, at most \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\) reinforcement queries are made throughout the algorithm. This yields a space bound of<tbc>

<tbc>\(\tilde{O}\left(min\left\{(\alpha(V)/k)^2,\alpha(V)\right\}\cdot 2k\right)\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)^{3/2}).\)<tbc>

• For cuts in step 3, the occupied space is at most \(\tilde{O}\left(\sum_{V^\prime}\alpha(V')+|V'|\right)\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\).

Altogether, the bound is \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)^{3/2})\), as required.

In order to obtain the data structure 2 of Theorem 3.1, we do not keep the separators from steps 1 and 6 as they were only used as witnesses. The total space bound is thus at most \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\), as required.

## 3.2 Our Reinforced Tree-Like Data Structure: A Las Vegas Version

In this section, we present a Las Vegas version of our algorithm, focusing on the differences from the Monte Carlo version presented above.

## Preprocessing

At a high level, the basic framework is similar and involves recursion. However, here we have _O_(log_n_) stages, and in each stage we focus on Max-Flow values that are in the range \[_k,_2_k_). In each stage the number of terminals, i.e., nodes _u_ such that \(\alpha(u)\ge k\), is at most \(\alpha(V)/k\). At the same time, the size of the optimal separators between node pairs in this stage is smaller than 2_k_. Consequently, if such pairs are in instances of size \(\ge 60klog^3n\) then many pivots can be chosen to separate them properly, which motivates making \(\tilde{O}(k)\) repetitions of the recursion tree (we may use the terms repetitions and recursion trees interchangeably) and arguing that a high enough number of pivots will be chosen throughout the repetitions. This will guarantee that each pair _u,v_ has at least one repetition where the corresponding pivot does not belong to _C<sub>uv</sub>_. The resulting partitions after running the \(\tilde{O}(k)\) repetitions will (almost) satisfy property (\*\*\*) that was discussed in Section 1.3.1. Indeed, we demonstrate that when the algorithm terminates, with _certainty_ for every _u,v_ query the correct answer can be obtained from one of the recursion trees, or that we have queried the pair _u,v_ directly.

Let us focus on a range \[_k,_2_k_), and set \(V_{\ge k}=\{u\in V:\alpha(u)\ge k\}\) as the set of terminals for the current stage. The following is the expansion operation on a subset of terminals \(V'\subseteq V_{\ge k}\). If \(V'=V_{\ge k}\) (i.e., in the beginning of the current stage) then repeat 60_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_ times.

1. pick a pivot node \(p\in V'\) uniformly at random.<tbc>

2. for every node \(u\in V'\backslash\{p\}\) perform a query Max-Flow(_p,u_) to get a vertex-cut (_S<sub>p,u</sub>,C<sub>p,u</sub>,S<sub>u,p</sub>_) where \(p\in S_{p,u}\), \(u\in S_{u,p}\), and the vertex-cut separating _u_ and _v_ (i.e. a _uv_-separator) is _C<sub>p,u</sub>_. Then, compute the intersection with \(V'\) of the side of _u_ in the cut, that is \(S_{u,p}\cap V'\), and denote this set by \(S'_{u,p}\), and similarly define \(S'_{p,u}\) and \(C'_{p,u}\).<tbc>

3. perform a reassignment process \(f:V'\rightarrow V'\cup\{\perp\}\) on the nodes \(V'\) and the corresponding cuts, similar to the Monte Carlo algorithm above, and set \(n'=|V'|\).<tbc>

4. if either<tbc>

(a) \(|V_{small}|<n'/4\), or<tbc>

(b) _p_ is an overused pivot, i.e., _p_ was selected as a pivot in 8log_n_ previous repetitions, then<tbc>

<tbc>_p_ is a failed pivot. In this situation, re-start the expansion operation at step 1 and continue choosing new pivots until both \(|V_{small}|\ge n'/4\) and _p_ not an overused pivot. We will show that with high probability, the number of pivot choices is _O_(log_n_).<tbc>

5. recursively compute the expansion operation on each set within the resulting partition whose size is larger than 60_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_. Let us describe what we store at the recursion node \(t_{V^\prime}\) corresponding to the just-completed expansion operation on \(V'\) with pivot _p_. We store \((|V'|-1)+\alpha(V')\) cuts in \(t_{V_{\ge k}^\prime}\), including:<tbc>

(a) for each \(u,v\in V'\) that we computed directly, we store _C<sub>u,v</sub>_.<tbc>

(b) for each node \(u_{big}\in V'_{big}\backslash\{p\}\) we store the cut (_S<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,C<sub>p,u<sub>big</sub></sub>,S<sub>u<sub>big</sub>,p</sub>_).<tbc>

(c) for each node _u_ in one of the other sets of the partition \(\{f^{-1}(i)\}_{i\in IM(f)}\) we store the cut it was reassigned to (_S<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>_,C<sub>p,f(u_)</sub>_,S<sub>f(u),p</sub>_).<tbc>

<tbc>We also keep an array of pointers from each node to its corresponding cuts and also their values, and we call this array _A_. We also store, for each node of \(V'\), the name of the set in the partition that it belongs to, in an array _B_.

6. finally, for every pair of nodes _u,v_ such that<tbc>

(a) \(u\in S_{f(v),p}\) (i.e., _u_ and _v_ are not separated) in the final instances of at least _k_ repetitions, or<tbc>

(b) \(u\in C_{p,f(v)}\) or \(v\in C_{p,f(u)}\) in at least _k_ repetitions,<tbc>

<tbc>query Max-Flow(_u,v_) directly.

## Queries

For data structure 1 of Theorem 3.1, to answer a query for a pair of nodes _u_ and _v_, we operate similarly to the Monte Carlo algorithm; first check if Max-Flow(_u,v_) was computed directly. If so, we output the corresponding separator, and otherwise we pick the answer with minimal value in the recursion trees that separated _u_ and _v_ in all relevant stages. The number of terminals in a \[_k,_2_k_\] stage is at most \(t_k=min\{\alpha(V)/k,n\}\), and so the total time to preprocess all node pairs in all stages and repetitions is \(\tilde{O}(max_k\left\{t_k^2\cdot k\right\})\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)n)\), bringing the query time to \(\tilde{O}(1)\), as required. On the bounds in data structure 2 of Theorem 3.1 we elaborate in the _Space usage_ paragraph, later in this section.

## Correctness

Let _u,v_ be any pair of nodes. We claim that if the pair _u,v_ is not queried directly, then it must be separated by a pivot _p_ such that \(p\notin C_{u,v}\), and then the correctness follows from the correctness proof in Section 3.1. Next, we bound the amount of times a single pivot is chosen throughout the algorithm.

**Lemma 3.6.** _With high probability, each pivot is chosen at most_ 8log_n times throughout all repetitions and depths._

_Proof._ Pivots are only chosen in instances of size greater than 60_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_, and each recursion depth has always at most 60_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_ instances containing _p_. As a result, the probability that the same pivot _p_ is chosen more than 8log_n_ times in the same recursion depth is at most 1_/n_<sup>6</sup>. By the union bound over all nodes, repetitions, and depths, with high probability no node is selected as a pivot more than 8log_n_ times, as required.

We say that a recursion tree becomes _invalid_ for a pair _u,v_ if _u_ and _v_ are separated in the tree (_u,v_ were assigned to different sets, i.e., \(f(u)\neq f(v)\)) but in a sub-optimal way, due to a pivot choice _p_ that belonged to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_. By Lemma 3.6, at every depth of the recursion at most 16_k_log_n_ recursion trees become invalid for the pair _u,v_. This is because the size of optimal separators in this stage is bounded by 2_k_. Since the height of the recursion tree is at most log<sub>4/3</sub>_n_ (see below), at the end of the recursion at least \(60klog^3n-16\cdot(1/log(4/3))\cdot klog^2n\ge 20klog^3n\) repetitions must not be invalid for _u,v_. In those 20_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_ remaining repetitions, one of the following three options must occur.

(i) _u_ and _v_ are not separated in the final instances of at least _k_ repetitions.<tbc>

(ii) \(u\in C_{p,v}\) (or \(v\in C_{p,u}\), symmetrically) in at least _k_ repetitions.<tbc>

(iii) _u_ and _v_ are separated \(\left(\text{i.e.,}u\in S_{f(u),p}\text{and}v\in S_{p,f(u)}\right)\) in at least one repetition by a pivot _p_ that does not belong to _C<sub>u,v</sub>_.

In cases (i) and (ii) we must have queried the pair _u,v_ directly in steps 6a and 6b, respectively. Otherwise, as the at most 2(_k_-1) repetitions where _u_ and _v_ fail to satisfy the requirements of step 6 can be identified, case (iii) occurs and we immediately have the right answer in a recursion tree.

To bound the height of the recursion trees, observe that Corollary 2.5 in \[AKT20a\], especially its adapted Corollary 3.5 mentioned above, is robust enough to accommodate the terminals, an aspect previously leveraged in those algorithms to handle the arbitrary node subsets resulting from the recursion. Thus, the same argument from the Monte Carlo algorithm on the height of the recursion trees being at most log<sub>4/3</sub>_n_ follows here as well. This concludes the correctness proof.

## Running time

A successful choice of a pivot _p_ in step 4 means that both (4a) \(|V_{small}|\ge n'/4\), and (4b) _p_ is not an overused pivot. The first case (4a) is handled similarly to the Monte Carlo algorithm; the probability of 8log_n_ consecutive failures in a single instance is bounded by (1/2)<sup>8log_n_</sup>=1_/n_<sup>8</sup>, and by applying the union bound over the at most \(\tilde{O}(n^2)\) instances in all repetitions, with probability at most 1_/n_<sup>6</sup> at least one instance takes more than 8log_n_ attempts until a successful choice of _p_. The second case (4b) was handled in the correctness proof in Lemma 3.6. Again, by the union bound over the two cases, with high probability no instance takes more than 8log_n_ times to select a pivot, and no pivots are overused. To bound the total number of Max-Flow calls, consider the total number of terminal pairs in all repetitions (counting multiplicities) for which we could potentially directly call Max-Flow.

• for case (i), this number is at most \(\tilde{O}((\alpha(V)/k)/k\cdot k^2\cdot k)\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)k)\). This is explained by having \((\alpha(V)/k)\) terminals in the \[_k,_2_k_) stage, considering only final (small) \(\le\tilde{O}(k)\) sized instances in this case, the at most \(\tilde{O}(k^2)\) pairs of terminals within a small instance, and the \(\tilde{O}(k)\) repetitions.<tbc>

• for case (ii), this number is simply bounded by \(\tilde{O}(\sum_{u\in V}\alpha(u)\cdot k)=\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)k)\).

Since we only call Max-Flow directly for a node pair if it is required by at least _k_ repetitions of a certain type (either (i), or (ii)), the total number of queries in both cases is bounded by \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\). The basic recursion takes \(\tilde{O}(k\cdot(\alpha(V)/k))\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\) calls to Max-Flow, concluding the running time proof.

## Space usage

We aim to bound the total space used by the data structure, starting with item 1 of Theorem 3.1.

• For cuts in step 2, an initial bound for the occupied space is at most<tbc>

<tbc>\(\tilde{O}\left(max_k\left\{k\cdot(min\{\alpha(V)/k,n\}\cdot 2k)\right\}\right)\le\tilde{O}(\alpha(V)n),\)<tbc>

<tbc>taking into account that for a cut \(\left(S_{p,f(u)},C_{p,f(u)},S_{f(u),p}\right)\) in this step and in a \[_k,_2_k_) stage, we only store the separator _C<sub>p,f(u_)</sub> if its size is smaller than 2_k_, and the set {_f_<sup>-1</sup>_f(u_)} (i.e., the nodes assigned to the side opposite of _p_). However, this can be further improved as all node pairs \(u,v\in V_{\ge k}\) are anyway queried directly for \(k\ge\sqrt{\alpha(V)/(60log^3n)}\) in step 6a due to the halting condition in step 5. Consequently, we may perform those queries directly in a preprocessing step, performing the recursion only for stages where \(k\le\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\alpha(V)}\right)\), and so the space occupied in step 2 becomes \(\tilde{O}\left(\alpha(V)^{3/2}\right)\), as required.<tbc>

• For cuts in step 6, recall that any query we make in this step is required by at least _k_ repetitions. Using the bound from the Monte Carlo algorithm, the occupied space here is at most<tbc>

<tbc>\(\tilde{O}\left(k\cdot\alpha(V)^{3/2}/k\right)\le\tilde{O}\left(\alpha(V)^{3/2}\right).\)<tbc>

Altogether, the bound is \(\tilde{O}\left(\alpha(V)^{3/2}\right)\), as required.

In order to obtain data structure 2 of Theorem 3.1, we do not store the separators from step 6 as they were only used as witnesses. However, we do maintain the list of \(\tilde{O}(\alpha(V))\) node pairs we directly called Max-Flow for in step 6, together with the corresponding answers. We further give up storing the separators from step 2, notwithstanding the immediate consequence that for a cut \(\left(S_{p,f(u)},C_{p,f(u)},S_{f(u),p}\right)\) and a node pair _u,v_ we cannot anymore immediately distinguish between the case where _u_ and _v_ are separated in the cut, i.e., \(v\in S_{p,f(u)}\), and the case where \(v\in C_{p,f(u)}\). However, we may assume that a direct Max-Flow(_u,v_) call was not made in step 6b (as we store the list of direct Max-Flow queries), and so it must be that this \(v\in C_{p,f(u)}\) case covered by step 6b, and also the case where \(v\in S_{f(u),p}\) in final instances covered by step 6a, happened in at most _k_-1 repetitions each. As established in the correctness proof, at least 20_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_ repetitions are not invalid for _u,v_ at the end of the recursion, and so at least \(20k\mathrm{log}^3n-2(k-1)\ge 18k\mathrm{log}^3n\) recursion trees must have the optimal answer for _u,v_. To find the optimal answer, simply take the majority among the smallest 19_k_log<sup>3</sup>_n_ answers, i.e., in repetitions where _u_ and _v_ do not belong together in final instances, concluding a query time of \(\tilde{O}(k)\) (as discussed before, node pairs in \[_k,_2_k_\] stages with \(k\ge\tilde{\Omega}\left(\sqrt{\alpha(V)}\right)\) can be answered faster, in \(\tilde{O}(1)\) time). The total space for data structure 2 is thus at most \(\tilde{O}\left(\alpha(V)\right)\), as required.

## 4 Conditional Lower Bound for Undirected Graphs with Unit Node- Capacities

Here, we show that the _n_<sup>3-_o_(1)</sup> conditional lower bound \[AKT20b\] for All-Pairs Max-Flow on undirected graphs with general node-capacities can be extended, using the source-sink isolating gadget presented in \[HLSW23\], to prove a conditional lower bound for undirected graphs with unit node- capacities.

**Lemma 4.1.** _3OV over vector sets of size n and dimension d can be reduced to All-Pairs Max-Flow on undirected graphs with_ \(\Theta(nd)\) _nodes,_ \(\Theta(n^2d^2)\) _edges, and unit node-capacities._

To see how Theorem 1.4 follows from Lemma 4.1, one can simply add isolated nodes and recall that the output is always of size \(\Theta(n^2)\).

_Proof of Lemma 4.1._ We generally follow the reduction from 3OV presented in \[AKT20b\], with minor modifications. As an intermediate construction in this reduction, a layered graph with undirected edges and a few directed edges was created. The following lemma describes the properties of this reduction, where ST-Max-Flow is a restricted version of All-Pairs Max-Flow focusing only on Max-Flow(_s,t_) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\), used here for convenience.

**Lemma 4.2** (From the proof of Lemma 4.2 in \[AKT20b\])**.** _3OV over vector sets of size n and dimension d can be reduced to ST-Max-Flow with_ |_S_|=|_T_|=_n in graphs G with_ \(\Theta(n\cdot d)\) _nodes,_ \(\Theta(n\cdot d)\) _edges, and with the following properties._

• _all nodes in_ \(S\cup T\) _have capacity_ 1_, and also_ \(\sum_{u\in V(G)}c(u)=O(nd)\).<tbc>

• _each edge_ \(uv\in E(G)\) _satisfies_ \(c(u)\cdot c(v)\le nd^2\).<tbc>

• _the edges adjacent to S are all directed away from S, and the edges adjacent to T are all directed towards T. The rest of the edges in G are undirected._<tbc>

It was shown that if an ST-Max-Flow algorithm could distinguish between the following two cases, then the input 3OV instance can be solved. In the first case, all pairs of nodes \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\) satisfy Max-Flow_<sub>G</sub>(s,t_)=_nd_, implying that there exists no orthogonal triple in the 3OV instance, i.e. it is a "NO" instance. In the second case, there exists at least one pair of nodes \(s'\in S\) and \(t'\in T\) such that \(\text{Max-Flow}_G(s',t')=nd-1\), indicating the presence of an orthogonal triple in the 3OV instance, i.e. it is a "YES" instance. In the final construction, all edges must become undirected. To prevent flows from zigzagging through _S_, and similarly through _T_, all node- capacities are multiplied by 2_n_, except for nodes in _S_ and _T_. It was then proved that the number of zigzagging flow paths in every _st_-flow is at most \(|(S\cup T)\backslash\{s,t\}|\le 2(n-1)\). Therefore, these paths can be disregarded after the node-capacities are multiplied by 2_n_.

We will show that an alternative way to increasing the capacities in _G_ is to use the source-sink gadget. However, before doing so, we need to modify the graph so that it only has unit node- capacities. This can be easily done by replacing each node _u_ with _c(u_) copies of itself, and by then adding a complete biclique between the new copies of _u_ and the new copies of _v_ for each edge \(uv\in G\). The resulting graph is denoted by \(G'\).

The number of nodes in \(G'\) is clearly \(\sum_{u\in V(G)}c(u)=O(nd)\), and the number of edges in \(G'\) is \(\sum_{uv\in E(G)}c(u)\cdot c(v)\le O(nd\cdot nd^2)=O(n^2d^3)\) (in fact, a more careful analysis leads to a bound of _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_d_<sup>2</sup>)). Importantly, for every \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\), every _st_-flow in _G_ naturally corresponds to an _st_-flow of the same value in \(G'\), and vice versa; to transform an _st_-flow in \(G'\) to an _st_-flow in _G_, simply contract nodes that correspond to the same node in _G_. Although the resulting flow may contain cycles, they can be disregarded.

Below is the source-sink isolating lemma, adapted to our notations.

**Lemma 4.3** (Lemma 3.2 in \[HLSW23\])**.** _Given an undirected graph R and two disjoint groups of vertices_ \(X,Y\subseteq V(R)\)_, there is a graph Q with_ \(V(Q)\cap V(R)=X\cup Y\) _such that for any_ \(x\in X,y\in Y\) _with_ \((x,y)\notin E(R)\),

\(\text{\textit{Max-Flow}}_{R\cup Q}(x,y)=\text{\textit{Max-Flow}}_{R_{xy}}(x,y)+|X|+|Y|,\)

_where_ \(R_{xy}=R\backslash((X\cup Y)\backslash\{x,y\})\)_. Such a graph P is called a source-sink isolating gadget and there is an algorithm that constructs Q with_ |_V(Q_)|=_O_(|_X_|+|_Y_|).

Constructing _Q_ can be easily done in linear time with respect to its size. We use Lemma 4.3, taking \(R=G'\), _X=S_ and _Y=T_. The lemma guarantees that \(\text{Max-Flow}_{G^\prime\cup Q}(s,t)=\text{Max-Flow}_{R_{st}}(s,t)+|S|+|T|\) for any \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\). Therefore, we can determine whether there exists an orthogonal triple by checking whether \(\text{Max-Flow}_{G^\prime}(s,t)=nd+2n\) for all \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\), or if there exists \(s'\in S\) and \(t'\in T\) such that \(\text{Max-Flow}_{G^\prime}(s',t')=nd-1+2n\).

The size of the graph remains asymptotically the same after adding the source-sink isolating gadget. Since All-Pairs Max-Flow is a more general problem than ST-Max-Flow, we can conclude Lemma 4.1.

## 5 Open Problems

After our work, many open problems on the fine-grained complexity of All-Pairs Max-Flow remain. Here are a few:

1. Can we break the _O(n_<sup>4</sup>) bound for any hard setting? With our new non-reducibility results, (non-combinatorial) subquartic algorithms seem more attainable.<tbc>

2. Can we establish a conditional lower bound of _n_<sup>2</sup>_m_<sup>1-_o_(1)</sup> for all _m_, against combinatorial algorithms? Such a lower bound is not known even for directed graphs with general edge capacities.<tbc>

3. Can we design an \(\hat{O}(m^2)\) time combinatorial algorithm for directed graphs with unit edge- capacities? Our adaptation of the framework in [AKT20a] may hint its robustness.<tbc>

4. Finally, the most significant open question after this work is: Can we design a subquartic nondeterministic algorithm for directed graphs with edge-capacities? Since our proof for the cut upper bounds in Lemma 2.2 holds for this setting too, it is enough to develop a fast nondeterministic algorithm that proves flow lower bounds.
